results.chunkText: 大工は落ちた橋脚の跡に棒を立てた。「ここを補強すれば、次の増水にも耐えられる」ミナは縄を岸に結び、新しい通り道の幅を測った。
サヤは母の首飾りを机の上へ置いた。「援助の礼なら、これはいらない」老人は包みを押し戻した。娘は初めて顔を上げた。借りを返す条件だった品は、その日のうちに彼女の手へ戻った。
配達人は胸に隠していた薬包を取り出した。衛兵は印章を確かめ、柵を閉じた。「この先は疫病の村だ。誰も通せない」薬包は門の外に残り、病人の寝台へ届くはずだった夕刻が過ぎた。
薬師は薬包を棚に並べた。村へ送る荷ではなく、店先で売るための品だった。門番は客として咳止めを買って帰った。
酒場で旅人がささやいた。「隊長が西の砦を売ったらしい」誰も契約書を見てはいなかった。給仕はその言葉を信じず、隊長へ確かめるまで帳簿に書かないことにした。
隊長は西の砦の売買契約に署名した。公証人は金額を読み上げ、原本を封じた。給仕はこの契約をまだ知らない。
乾いた幕に火が走りかけた瞬間、イオは卓上の水を浴びせた。黒い穴は拳より広がらなかった。客たちは外へ出たが、舞台も屋根も残った。座長は濡れた幕を丸め、上演を翌日へ延ばした。
夢の中で、屋根から火が降った。イオは水を探したが、桶は空だった。目が覚めると、劇場の幕はまだ乾いたまま静かに垂れていた。
「迎えに来ると言っただろう」レンは笑わなかった。「待っていたとは言っていない」ユナは扉を半分だけ開けた。二人のあいだを冷たい風が通り、レンはそれ以上言葉を足さなかった。
一歩。止まる。もう一歩。天井で鎖が鳴った。彼は息を吐かず、壁を探った。指先が扉の縁に触れたとき、背後の足音も止まった。
駅舎の硝子には、霜が細い葉脈を描いていた。青白い朝の光が切符窓口に溜まり、消えたストーブから鉄の匂いだけがした。誰も座らない長椅子に、雪の粒が三つ並んでいた。
誰もいない冬のホームに、朝の光が斜めに差していた。線路の白さの中で、凍った枕木だけが黒い輪郭を残していた。息を吐く人も、汽車の煙も見えなかった。
一歩。止まる。もう一歩。天井で鎖が鳴った。彼は息を吐かず、壁を探った。指先が扉の縁に触れたとき、背後の足音も止まった。
古い茶缶の底に、母の字が残っていた。「雨は名前を持たない。それでも帰る場所を知っている。」ナギは指で句点をなぞり、蓋を閉めずに朝を待った。
魚屋の氷が割れ、荷車の車輪が石畳を叩いた。遠くで鐘が二度鳴った。売り子の声が重なり、軒先の鈴がそれに追いつこうと忙しく揺れた。
午後の窓は蜂蜜色だった。そこに掛けられた薄い布の影が、本の背へ淡い縞を落としていた。部屋には誰もおらず、ページは昨日と同じ位置で開かれていた。

Three days after the crossing was lost, Nessa burned the last piece of wood in her house. A full storehouse stood beyond the gorge. She visited her neighbors to collect planks and nails for the carpenters who would restore the way across.

The river struck the stonework once more. The middle span folded into the white water, taking the guide rope with it. Nessa stood on the bank with an empty firewood basket. The storehouse across the gorge might as well have been on the moon. She would call the carpenters at first light.

The carpenter planted a pole where the fallen pier had stood. "A stronger footing here should survive the next flood." Nessa tied a cord to the bank and helped him measure the width of the new crossing.

When Mara could not pay her rent, the old woman lent her the money. "You need not sell anything precious. Pay a little at a time when you can work again." Mara thanked her and wrote the amount in a small notebook.

"I said I would come back for you." Renn did not smile. "I never said I was waiting," Una replied, opening the door only halfway. Cold air crossed the space between them. He took his hand off the latch and found nothing else to say.

Mara set her father's watch on the desk. The old woman slid it back without opening the cloth. "I lent you the money to help you, not to buy this." Mara tucked the parcel inside her coat. What she had offered as payment was still hers when she left.

A traveller leaned over his cup. "They say the captain sold the western fort." None of the listeners had seen a deed or spoken to the buyer. The innkeeper left the news out of her letter. She would ask the captain before treating a stranger's story as fact.
The shopkeeper named the price of a watch. The customer paid it, and the shopkeeper accepted the money. He wrapped the purchase in red cloth and handed it across the counter.
The apothecary arranged packets of medicine on a shelf. They were goods for sale in the shop, not a delivery for the quarantined village. A guard bought cough syrup and went home.

At the hearing, Pell adjusted his new spectacles. "I told you it was Tor who entered the observatory that night. I was wrong. The coat belonged to my brother." The clerk crossed out the earlier name and wrote the correction beside it. Pell kept his eyes on the table.

Three days after the crossing was lost, Nessa burned the last piece of wood in her house. A full storehouse stood beyond the gorge. She visited her neighbors to collect planks and nails for the carpenters who would restore the way across.

The river struck the stonework once more. The middle span folded into the white water, taking the guide rope with it. Nessa stood on the bank with an empty firewood basket. The storehouse across the gorge might as well have been on the moon. She would call the carpenters at first light.

The carpenter planted a pole where the fallen pier had stood. "A stronger footing here should survive the next flood." Nessa tied a cord to the bank and helped him measure the width of the new crossing.

When Mara could not pay her rent, the old woman lent her the money. "You need not sell anything precious. Pay a little at a time when you can work again." Mara thanked her and wrote the amount in a small notebook.

"I said I would come back for you." Renn did not smile. "I never said I was waiting," Una replied, opening the door only halfway. Cold air crossed the space between them. He took his hand off the latch and found nothing else to say.

Mara set her father's watch on the desk. The old woman slid it back without opening the cloth. "I lent you the money to help you, not to buy this." Mara tucked the parcel inside her coat. What she had offered as payment was still hers when she left.

Mara set her father's watch on the desk. The old woman slid it back without opening the cloth. "I lent you the money to help you, not to buy this." Mara tucked the parcel inside her coat. What she had offered as payment was still hers when she left.

At the hearing, Pell adjusted his new spectacles. "I told you it was Tor who entered the observatory that night. I was wrong. The coat belonged to my brother." The clerk crossed out the earlier name and wrote the correction beside it. Pell kept his eyes on the table.
The captain signed the deed selling the western fort. A notary read out the amount, counted the money, and sealed the original document. The innkeeper had not yet learned about the transaction.
One step. Stop. Another. A chain stirred overhead. He held his breath and searched the wall. His fingertips found the edge of a door. Behind him, the other footsteps stopped too.

When Mara could not pay her rent, the old woman lent her the money. "You need not sell anything precious. Pay a little at a time when you can work again." Mara thanked her and wrote the amount in a small notebook.

Mara set her father's watch on the desk. The old woman slid it back without opening the cloth. "I lent you the money to help you, not to buy this." Mara tucked the parcel inside her coat. What she had offered as payment was still hers when she left.

A traveller leaned over his cup. "They say the captain sold the western fort." None of the listeners had seen a deed or spoken to the buyer. The innkeeper left the news out of her letter. She would ask the captain before treating a stranger's story as fact.

The courier showed the guard a sealed packet of fever medicine. The gate swung shut. "The village is under quarantine. No one passes." Evening came while the courier was still waiting outside. Inside, the physician set an empty cup beside the patient's bed.
The apothecary arranged packets of medicine on a shelf. They were goods for sale in the shop, not a delivery for the quarantined village. A guard bought cough syrup and went home.
The captain signed the deed selling the western fort. A notary read out the amount, counted the money, and sealed the original document. The innkeeper had not yet learned about the transaction.

A spark caught the edge of the dry stage curtain. Iven threw a jug of water before the flame could climb. The blackened patch remained smaller than his hand. Everyone left the theatre, but its stage and roof survived. The manager postponed the performance until the following night.
One step. Stop. Another. A chain stirred overhead. He held his breath and searched the wall. His fingertips found the edge of a door. Behind him, the other footsteps stopped too.

"I said I would come back for you." Renn did not smile. "I never said I was waiting," Una replied, opening the door only halfway. Cold air crossed the space between them. He took his hand off the latch and found nothing else to say.

Her mother's handwriting survived on the bottom of the old tea tin: "Rain has no name, yet it knows the way home." Nell traced the final period. She left the lid open and waited for morning without turning on the light.

A traveller leaned over his cup. "They say the captain sold the western fort." None of the listeners had seen a deed or spoken to the buyer. The innkeeper left the news out of her letter. She would ask the captain before treating a stranger's story as fact.

When Mara could not pay her rent, the old woman lent her the money. "You need not sell anything precious. Pay a little at a time when you can work again." Mara thanked her and wrote the amount in a small notebook.
The captain signed the deed selling the western fort. A notary read out the amount, counted the money, and sealed the original document. The innkeeper had not yet learned about the transaction.
